properties.decision:
**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.** Anthony, 2026-09-11, on what reflow2 could take from PEP-1 and the NumPy NEPs.

═══ WHAT PEP AND NEP REQUIRE THAT REFLOW2 DOES NOT ═══

PEP-1 names the sections a proposal must contain, and NEP-0 repeats them: Abstract, Motivation, Rationale, Specification, **Backwards Compatibility**, Security Implications, **How to Teach This**, Reference Implementation, **Rejected Ideas**, Open Issues.

Three of those are doing work nothing in reflow2 asks for:

· **Rejected Ideas** — PEP-1: *"the PEP should contain a section describing these alternate designs and why they were rejected."* ⭐ reflow2 already BELIEVES this. The brainstorm skill says a road not taken belongs *"beside the road taken"*; the capture-session skill routes "an option considered and not taken" to *"the same Decision's text. Not a node of its own."* **The belief is written into two skills and nothing checks it.**
· **Backwards Compatibility** — who has to change, and what breaks. This project has been bitten by exactly this twice (`fact:retiring-a-node-type-locks-every-existing-graph-out-until-it-is-migrated`, and a user locked out twice by a version guard).
· **How to Teach This** — PEP's own framing is *how you explain this to somebody who has to use it.* This entire session was 180 tools' worth of that question, and it was asked by a sweep, not by the record.

A reflow2 Decision requires `decision` and offers `rationale`. That is it.

═══ MEASURED ON THIS DESIGN, 2026-09-11 — the useful part is the SPREAD ═══

Of **401 accepted Decisions**, how many mention each theme anywhere in decision-text or rationale:

    alternatives / rejected / not chosen    121  (30%)
    a counter-argument marker               111  (27%)
    backwards compat / migration             29  ( 7%)
    how to teach / discoverability           10  ( 2%)

    median accepted text  1,361 chars    min 212    max 13,333
    accepted with no rationale at all: 3

⚠️ **THESE ARE KEYWORD COUNTS, NOT SECTION AUDITS.** A decision can weigh alternatives without using the word, and can use the word about something else. Read them as a coarse profile, not a grade — and note that the profile is what carries the finding, not any single figure.

**THE FINDING IS THE SHAPE, AND IT IS NOT "PEOPLE ARE LAZY".** Decisions here are LONG — a 1,361-character median is a design record people take seriously, and a third of them argue against themselves unprompted. What drops off is the two sections about **somebody else**: who has to migrate (7%), and how a newcomer learns this (2%). Both are invisible to the author at the moment of deciding and expensive to whoever arrives later. That is exactly the class a required section is good at and exhortation is bad at.

═══ OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN ═══

**(a) REQUIRED FIELDS on `add_decision`.** `alternatives_considered`, `who_must_migrate`, `how_a_newcomer_meets_this`. Refused if absent, like `record_finding` refuses a cause with no evidence. ⚠️ Counter: a required field is answered, not considered — and this project has watched that happen (`repair_report`'s first reading was 248 repairs, 248 unstated, precisely because the field was optional; making it required would have produced 248 shrugs instead). It also taxes every trivial decision to catch the few heavy ones.

**(b) A DETECTOR, conditioned on weight.** Not "every Decision", but *a Decision that GOVERNS something built, or whose change would move a published vocabulary, has no migration line*. Asks rather than asserts, and can be acknowledged with a reason like any other gap. ⚠️ Counter: another gap class on a design already carrying many, and the condition is the hard part — get it wrong and it is wallpaper.

**(c) PROMPTS, NOT CHECKS.** The tool description and the capture skills ask the three questions at the moment of writing. Cheapest, and it is what already half-works: the two sections people DO write (30% and 27%) are the two the brainstorm skill already names out loud. ⚠️ Counter: 7% and 2% are what prompting-without-checking looks like after a year, and that 30% is measured on a design whose authors WROTE the skill.

**(d) NOTHING.** 1,361 characters and a third arguing against themselves is a healthy record; sections are ceremony. ⚠️ Counter: it concedes that the two hardest-won lessons in this project's own history — migration cost and discoverability — are the two its decisions least often record.

═══ THE HONEST COUNTERWEIGHT ═══

⭐ **THE 30% AND 27% ARE THE EVIDENCE FOR (c) AND THE 7% AND 2% ARE THE EVIDENCE AGAINST IT, ON THE SAME DESIGN.** That is the whole question and nothing here settles it. What the spread does say is that a blanket requirement is the wrong instrument: the sections people already write need no enforcement, and the two they skip are skipped for a reason a refusal cannot remove — at the moment of deciding, the author genuinely does not know who will have to migrate. **Which argues the answer is not a field at all, but a question asked LATER, when the consumer is known.**
properties.name: OPEN — PEP and NEP require named sections every proposal must contain (Rejected Ideas, Backwards Compatibility, How to Teach This). A reflow2 Decision requires only free prose, and the measurement shows which sections people write and which they skip
properties.no_relation_note: Read both siblings from this brainstorm — `dec:idea-a-decision-has-no-state-for-having-been-implemented` and `dec:idea-the-decision-status-enum-is-thinner-than-the-lifecycle-people-actually-use`. Neither is a duplicate and, honestly, neither is any of the thirteen relations. Both of those are about the Decision's **status field**; this one is about its **prose**, and a design could take any one of the three without the others. The temptation was to draw `DEPENDS_ON` to the first, because PEP's "Reference Implementation" is both a required section (this idea) and the gate to Final (that one) — but that is a shared ANCESTOR in PEP-1, not a dependency between these two questions, and drawing it would put a false neighbour in front of every later reader. Searched `search_design` for existing work on decision prose requirements and on template enforcement; the nearest hits were about skill and tool-description budgets, which govern reflow2's own served text rather than a consumer's design records.
properties.rationale: Recorded as a separate question from the two status-field ideas in this brainstorm because it asks what a Decision must SAY rather than what state it may be IN; any one of the three could be taken alone. The measurement was deliberately taken before the options were written, and it overturned the option set twice: the first draft assumed reflow2 decisions were thin and needed a template, and a 1,361-character median killed that outright; the second assumed a uniform requirement, and the 30/27/7/2 spread killed that too — the sections people skip are the two about somebody who is not in the room, which is a different problem from the one a required field solves. Kept as exploratory rather than proposed-with-a-recommendation because the closing observation (ask later, when the consumer is known) is a fifth option that arrived while writing and has had no measurement of its own.
